subject: design-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is a design brief?
options: A short statement outlining the design problem to be solved and what is required
A detailed working drawing showing exact dimensions of the final product
A list of the tools and machines needed to manufacture a product
A written evaluation of a finished product against its specification
questions.explain: A design brief is a concise statement that sets out the problem, the client or user needs and the purpose of the product.

questions.q: Which of these is normally the FIRST stage of the design process?
options: Identifying a need or problem
Manufacturing the final product
Writing the design specification
Producing developed design ideas
questions.explain: The design process begins by identifying a need or problem before any research or designing takes place.

questions.q: The design process is often described as 'iterative'. What does this mean?
options: Stages can be repeated and revisited, with ideas refined through cycles of testing and improvement
Every stage must be completed once, strictly in order, with no going back
The designer works entirely alone without any user feedback
Only one solution is produced and it cannot be changed
questions.explain: An iterative process loops back through stages so ideas are continually tested, evaluated and improved.

questions.q: What is primary research?
options: Collecting new, first-hand data yourself, for example through surveys or product testing
Using data already published by others, such as books or websites
Manufacturing a prototype to test a mechanism
Sketching a range of initial design ideas
questions.explain: Primary research is original data gathered directly by the designer, such as questionnaires, interviews or user trials.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of SECONDARY research?
options: Reading information from books, magazines and websites
Carrying out a face-to-face interview with a user
Handing out a questionnaire to potential customers
Testing a product with a focus group
questions.explain: Secondary research uses existing, already-published sources rather than data the designer gathers first-hand.

questions.q: Why might a designer choose a questionnaire rather than a one-to-one interview when researching a product?
options: It can gather responses from a large number of people quickly and be analysed easily
It always produces more detailed and personal answers than any other method
It removes the need to write a design specification
It guarantees that every person will answer truthfully
questions.explain: Questionnaires reach many people efficiently and closed questions make the results easy to collate and compare.

questions.q: What does the term 'anthropometrics' refer to?
options: The study and use of measurements of the human body
The strength and durability of materials
The cost of manufacturing a product in batches
The visual appearance and style of a product
questions.explain: Anthropometrics is the collection and application of human body measurement data when designing products.

questions.q: Ergonomics is best described as designing products so that they are:
options: Comfortable, efficient and safe for people to use
As cheap as possible to manufacture
Made only from recycled materials
Attractive in colour and decoration
questions.explain: Ergonomics focuses on the relationship between people and products so items are comfortable, efficient and safe in use.

questions.q: A designer uses anthropometric data based on the 5th to 95th percentile range. Why is this range used?
options: So the product suits the majority of users, excluding only the extreme smallest and largest
So the product only fits the single average-sized person
So the product is made as cheaply as possible
So the product suits every single person without exception
questions.explain: Designing for the 5th–95th percentile fits about 90% of users, a practical compromise rather than trying to suit everyone.

questions.q: What is a design specification?
options: A list of criteria or requirements that the finished product must meet
A freehand sketch of an early design idea
A schedule listing the order of manufacturing operations
A survey used to collect the views of potential users
questions.explain: The design specification sets out the measurable criteria and requirements a successful product must satisfy.

questions.q: Which specification point is the MOST useful because it can be measured and tested?
options: The product must support a mass of at least 20 kg without bending
The product should look nice and modern
The product must be a good size for people
The product should be reasonably strong
questions.explain: A good specification point is specific and measurable, allowing the finished product to be objectively tested against it.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a mood board?
options: To gather images, colours and textures that communicate a style, theme or feeling
To show the exact dimensions of a product
To list the manufacturing costs of a product
To record test results from user trials
questions.explain: A mood board collects visual references such as images, colours and textures to explore and communicate a design theme.

questions.q: Brainstorming (mind mapping) is mainly used to:
options: Quickly generate a large number of initial ideas without judging them
Produce accurate scale drawings of the final design
Test the strength of the chosen material
Write the final evaluation of the product
questions.explain: Brainstorming encourages a free flow of many ideas early on, deferring judgement to maximise creative output.

questions.q: Why is it important to add annotation (notes) to design sketches?
options: To explain features, materials and reasoning so ideas can be judged and developed
To make the page look fuller and more colourful
To replace the need for any drawing at all
To hide weaknesses in the design idea
questions.explain: Annotation communicates the thinking behind a sketch — materials, functions and pros and cons — so ideas can be evaluated and developed.

questions.q: What does a morphological analysis (morphological chart) help a designer to do?
options: Combine different options for each feature of a product to create new possible solutions
Calculate the exact cost of manufacturing
Record human body measurements
Evaluate a finished product against its specification
questions.explain: A morphological chart lists possible options for each function and combines them to generate a range of new solutions.

questions.q: During development, a designer makes a card model of a proposed product. What is the main benefit of modelling before final manufacture?
options: It lets the designer test scale, form and function and spot problems cheaply before committing
It guarantees the product will sell well
It removes the need to write a specification
It replaces the need for any testing of the final product
questions.explain: Modelling allows a design to be tested and refined quickly and cheaply before investing time and materials in the final product.

questions.q: A student is designing a lamp for a child's bedroom. Which research task would give the MOST relevant primary data about the users?
options: Surveying parents and children about how and where they would use a bedroom lamp
Reading a website about the history of lighting
Copying the specification of an existing adult desk lamp
Looking up the melting point of the plastic to be used
questions.explain: Surveying the actual users generates first-hand primary data directly relevant to the target market's needs.

questions.q: A designer has produced several rough initial ideas. What is the BEST next step to move towards a final design?
options: Select promising ideas and develop them further with detailed sketches, modelling and annotation
Immediately manufacture the very first idea drawn
Delete all the ideas and start the brief again
Write the product evaluation before making anything
questions.explain: Development means refining the most promising initial ideas through further sketching, modelling and annotation before finalising.

questions.q: When evaluating a finished product, what should it mainly be judged against?
options: The points listed in the design specification
The personal taste of the designer only
The cost of the tools used to make it
The number of ideas generated at the start
questions.explain: Evaluation checks how well the outcome meets each measurable criterion set out in the design specification.

questions.q: A company wants a new product aimed at teenagers. Identifying the 'target market' will mainly help the designer to:
options: Make design decisions such as style, cost and features suited to that group of users
Decide which machine tools to buy for the workshop
Choose the order of manufacturing operations
Calculate the melting temperature of the material
questions.explain: Knowing the target market guides choices of appearance, function, price and features so the product appeals to its intended users.
